sources.title: Tadao Ando (Q208220) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-23): English label 'Tadao Ando', description 'Japanese architect (born 1941)', born 13 September 1941, no date of death, citizenship Japan, Korean label '안도 다다오', P18 image 'Tadao Ando 2004.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

The Pritzker Architecture Prize, 'Tadao Ando -- Laureate 1995' page (pritzkerprize.com), read in full: the jury citation (work as 'an assemblage of artistically composed surprises in space and form'; a 'powerful inner vision' that ignores passing movements, schools and styles; linked to international Modernism and the Japanese aesthetic tradition), Jay A. Pritzker's remark that Ando 'conceives his projects as places of habitation not as abstract designs in a landscape' (presentation on 22 May 1995 at Versailles), and the laureate biography: woodworking learned from a carpenter as a boy, a brief boxing stint, short apprenticeships, self-study of temples, shrines and teahouses in Kyoto and Nara, study trips to Europe and the United States in the 1960s with detailed sketching, a secondhand Le Corbusier book whose drawings he traced until the pages 'turned black' (self), and a description of his method (thick concrete walls, basic geometry, watertight varnished wooden formwork for a smooth finish, evenly spaced formwork bolt holes left visible, light as a central element) with a list of works (Azuma House 1977, Church on the Water 1988, Church of the Light 1989, Naoshima Contemporary Art Museum 1992, Japan Pavilion Expo '92, Rokko Housing). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (award body; admiring institutional record). The speech texts it links to were not opened.

Encyclopedia.com compilation of reference entries 'Ando, Tadao' (Gale 'Newsmakers 2005 Cumulation' and 'Encyclopedia of World Biography', and James Stevens Curl's 'A Dictionary of Architecture and Landscape Architecture', Oxford), read in full: professional boxing at 17 after his twin brother, travels in Japan, Europe and the United States (Oxford adds Africa), carpenter apprenticeship, self-training through the four-year architecture-student reading list in one year, being dismissed from apprenticeships for 'stubbornness and temper' (self-reported, 1993/2005 interview material), opening his practice in Osaka in 1969 rather than Tokyo, the Row House in Sumiyoshi (Azuma House, 1976; Architectural Institute of Japan annual prize 1979), his habit of pressing clients to accept unconventional designs, high-quality cast concrete, comparisons with Kahn, Le Corbusier and Mies, and critiques (Manchester Piccadilly Gardens mixed reviews, a 'defensive' inward-turning architecture, 'domesticated' nature). Independent reference compilation with some critical notes; some dates differ between entries (Azuma House 1976 vs 1977/1979), so only the Gale 1976 date is used here.

Kieran Long, 'Tadao Ando' profile, Icon magazine (issue 039, September 2006; online 2007), read in full: a critical profile written after a London press breakfast following his City of London Festival lecture -- no formal architectural education, a 1965 trip to Paris by Trans-Siberian express to meet Le Corbusier (arriving weeks after his death), his early Osaka schemes repeatedly rejected by city authorities, his statement that there is 'no direct correlation' between architecture and boxing 'except that you're on your own', his corporate clients (Novartis in Basel, Armani in Milan), the Omotesando Hills redevelopment for developer Minoru Mori (137 dwellings and one shop in the 1927 Dojunkai apartments replaced by 38 dwellings and 93 commercial units, per critic Julian Worrall), the author's view that the 'perfect concrete' look now seems familiar and cold, and an account of Ando ending the interview abruptly ('I don't understand your questions'). Critical, independent press voice; the author's comments on Ando's manner are interview-room impressions and are not used as a character judgement.

Google Arts & Culture story 'Early Life' on Tadao Ando (artsandculture.google.com), read in full: raised by his grandmother in an Osaka neighbourhood of woodworkers and metalworkers, building from scrap wood, a roof-hole light episode he treats as the origin of his architecture (self-attributed), boxing from high school with a professional debut at 17 and quitting after watching Fighting Harada spar, self-study while working at interior and furniture design firms, a 1960s European trip by ship and the Trans-Siberian Railway to see the Parthenon, the Pantheon and Le Corbusier's buildings, founding his Osaka studio in 1969, the Urban Guerrilla Houses (1972; only the Tomishima House, 1973, built) and the Row House in Sumiyoshi (1976) that brought him wide recognition, and his insistence that 'architects are made through traveling' (self). Institutional digital-exhibit narrative, admiring; the publisher partner of the story was not verified and its dates for the European trip differ from other sources (1964 vs 1965), so trip dates are not relied on.

'An Architect's Paradise: The Hidden Treasures of Tadao Ando's Art Island', Architizer Journal (by 'The Angry Architect'; undated), read in full: Ando's Naoshima buildings -- the Chichu Art Museum, largely sunk into the hillside, where 'every piece of art would be lit by natural light sources' with rooms designed around specific works by Monet, Walter De Maria and James Turrell; the Benesse House Museum; the Lee Ufan Museum, where the artist wanted a gallery wall white against Ando's preference for grey; and the Ando Museum inserting concrete planes inside a traditional timber house. Independent architecture-press travel feature, admiring in tone; no construction years or commissioning details given.

Cat Garcia Menocal, 'tadao ando's green wall of hope incites controversy', designboom, 27 June 2013, read in full: Ando's planned 78-metre green wall (stainless-steel net, 900 planters) in the grounds of the Shin Umeda City complex in Osaka; landscape architect Motoo Yoshimura, who designed the ground-level garden, filed a petition to suspend construction, arguing it would fundamentally change the identity of his garden and violate copyright law. No response from Ando is reported and no outcome is given. Independent trade-press report of a professional dispute; one-sided in what it reports.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Tadao Ando 2004.jpg' (wikitext and API record) -- checked for the portrait's licence: photograph by Christopher Schriner (Cologne), taken September 2004 at the opening of the Langen Foundation exhibition building, Germany; Flickr source passed an automated Flickr licence review on 6 January 2011 as CC BY-SA 2.0; original 683 x 1024 pixels. Not used for any scoring.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_ando_pritzker, src_ando_gale, src_ando_icon, src_ando_gac | 1960s-1990s | award-body citation + reference compilation + critical profile + exhibit narrative] With no formal architectural training he built his own curriculum (the architecture-student reading list in one year, per the Gale entries), study journeys and sketchbooks (Pritzker, Google Arts & Culture), and opened his practice in Osaka in 1969 rather than in Tokyo (Gale). The Pritzker jury credits a 'powerful inner vision' that ignores passing movements, schools and styles, and Icon notes that his early Osaka schemes were repeatedly rejected by city authorities. Four sources agree on a self-directed route and an individual formal language; part of this is his own account (the reading list, the dismissals) and the citation is admiring, so documented at a moderate confidence.

persistence.rationale: [src_ando_gale, src_ando_icon, src_ando_gac | 1969-1976 | reference compilation + critical profile + exhibit narrative] After leaving boxing and being dismissed from apprenticeships (his own account in the Gale entries) he kept working in interior and furniture firms while teaching himself (Google Arts & Culture), opened his own office at 28, and pursued experimental schemes in Osaka that, per Icon, the city authorities repeatedly rejected, before the Row House in Sumiyoshi (1976) brought wide recognition and the Architectural Institute of Japan annual prize in 1979 (Gale). A long, dated path from outsider to recognised architect is described by three sources, but the early-years detail rests partly on his own retellings and the rejected-schemes line is a single sentence, so a moderate confidence.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_ando_pritzker, src_ando_gale, src_ando_architizer | 1970s-2000s | award-body biography + reference compilation + press feature] Pritzker's laureate biography emphasises that he values the precision of the formwork over the concrete mix itself, uses watertight varnished wooden forms for a smooth finish, and leaves evenly spaced bolt holes as a deliberate mark; Gale describes a lustrous, very high-quality cast concrete, and Architizer reports that every artwork in the Chichu Art Museum was to be lit by natural light, with rooms designed around specific works. Three sources describe the same exacting construction and detailing across decades; they are admiring, but the craft specifics are concrete and checkable, so documented.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_ando_pritzker, src_ando_gale, src_ando_gac, src_ando_icon | 1972-2000s | award-body citation + reference compilation + exhibit narrative + critical profile] The Pritzker citation describes 'artistically composed surprises in space and form'; the Row House in Sumiyoshi (1976) is described in Gale as a two-storey house just over three metres wide with a windowless concrete front and a roofless central courtyard that residents must cross to move between rooms, which Ando defends as making residents aware of weather and place; Google Arts & Culture cites the earlier Urban Guerrilla Houses concept (1972) and the Church of the Light and Church on the Water are named by Pritzker. Icon, a critical source, accepts the distinctiveness while arguing the look later became familiar elsewhere. Distinctive formal invention is credited by an award body, a reference work and a critic, so documented, with confidence limited by mostly admiring sources.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_ando_pritzker, src_ando_architizer, src_ando_gale | 1989-2004 | award-body biography + press feature + reference compilation] Pritzker names light as central to his work and lists the Church of the Light (1989); Architizer describes the Chichu Art Museum buried in the hillside so the art is lit only by natural light, and Gale says he leaves walls undecorated and relies on changing sunlight and shadow. Sustained attention to light and spatial atmosphere is shown across several projects, but the evidence is descriptive and largely admiring rather than a specific recorded decision, so strong inference at a moderate confidence.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_ando_gale, src_ando_architizer, src_ando_designboom, src_ando_icon | 1970s-2013 | reference compilation + press feature + trade-press report + critical profile] Gale says he kept pressing clients to accept unconventional designs; Architizer recounts a disagreement with Lee Ufan over the colour of a gallery wall at the Lee Ufan Museum (Ando preferred grey, the artist white); designboom reports that landscape architect Motoo Yoshimura petitioned to halt Ando's 2013 green-wall addition in Osaka as a copyright violation (no response or outcome reported); Icon describes him ending a press interview abruptly. The pattern shows willingness to hold his position, but each item is a single brief report, one is a one-sided allegation, and the outcomes are unknown, so strong inference at a lower confidence, dual-edged.

curiosity.rationale: [src_ando_pritzker, src_ando_gac, src_ando_icon | 1960s | award-body biography + exhibit narrative + critical profile] Pritzker says he studied temples, shrines and teahouses in Kyoto and Nara and made study trips to Europe and the United States, sketching buildings in detail and keeping sketchbooks; Google Arts & Culture describes a long overland journey to see the Parthenon, the Pantheon and Le Corbusier's buildings, and Icon records the Paris trip. Self-funded study travel and detailed sketching are well attested, but the travel dates differ between sources and the framing ('architects are made through traveling') is his own, so strong inference at a modest confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 70 / 0.52 lowered to 66 / 0.48 because trip dates conflict across sources and the interpretive framing is self-reported.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-23) for Q208220 returned en label 'Tadao Ando', description 'Japanese architect (born 1941)', born 1941-09-13, no death date, citizenship Japan (Q17), kowiki label '안도 다다오', P18 'Tadao Ando 2004.jpg'; the lead's hint was correct. SLUG/QID CHECK: no candidate or production file for slug tadao-ando or QID Q208220 in the roster53 worktree. REGION: east_asia, nationality JP. VOCABULARY: occupation architect, field architecture, impact domains artistic and cultural, tags self_taught, career_changer, craft_focused, independent and archetype creative_creator are existing ids used by other candidates (e.g. Alvar Aalto). ZERO POLITICS: nothing political scored or carded. LIVING SUBJECT: only documented professional work and public professional conduct is scored. EXCLUDED deliberately: family and upbringing details beyond the work-formation story, health, the New National Stadium competition and its cost controversy (public-body role, not opened), the Omotesando Hills debate beyond what Icon reports, and the Wikipedia/Wikidata pages (orientation only). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: The Pritzker Architecture Prize 1995 laureate page (https://www.pritzkerprize.com/laureates/1995; read in full). READ (7 cited non-Wikidata sources): Pritzker page, Encyclopedia.com Gale/Oxford compilation, Icon 2006 profile, Google Arts & Culture story, Architizer Naoshima feature, designboom 2013 report, Commons file page. Britannica returned HTTP 403 and the Tokyo Weekender interview returned HTTP 522, so neither was read or cited. PERSPECTIVES: award-body jury and biography (admiring); independent reference compilation with critical notes; critical trade press (Icon: cold repetition, defensiveness, Omotesando Hills; designboom: copyright dispute); exhibit narrative; architecture travel press; Ando's own remarks (self; relayed by Pritzker, Gale, Icon and Google Arts, never sole support). SELF-ACCOUNT CAVEAT: the boxer-turned-self-taught-architect story is told by Pritzker's biography, the Gale entries and Google Arts & Culture, all drawing on his own accounts; details differ (boxing span, trip dates, Azuma House year), so only the broad, consistent outline is carded and no specific date for the trip or boxing is asserted. COUNTER-VOICES: Icon, the Oxford and Gale critiques (defensive, domesticated nature, Manchester), and designboom's Yoshimura petition. CALIBRATION: sources are mostly admiring or self-derived and behavioural episodes are brief, so the highest score is 78 and the highest confidence 0.60; seven rows, none padded. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed the three highest-risk rows (creative_originality, independent_thinking, conflict_tolerance); creative_originality and independent_thinking left unchanged (corroborated by an award body, a reference work and a critical source); conflict_tolerance was already set low and dual-edged because each item is a single brief report; curiosity lowered from 70 / 0.52 to 66 / 0.48 (conflicting trip dates, self-framed claim). PORTRAIT: Commons 'Tadao Ando 2004.jpg', creator Christopher Schriner, CC BY-SA 2.0, 683x1024, no conflicting institutional notice (privately held Flickr source with passed licence review); a different Commons upload from the same Flickr set was not needed.
